It's a blatant mischaracterization. Now, this was before I was hired, but I'm a former Origin employee, and I worked on UO, and the sadly canceled UO2. Nobody was upset that Rainz killed Richard Garriot's character. Hell, killing Lord British was an easter egg in many of the Ultima games, and trying to kill him to be expected and celebrated. Why Origin came down hard on him was because he was part of a very dedicated group of players who specialized in exploits...and they were the bane of our existence.

I would say that more money was spent on trying to foil exploiters and cheaters than on the game itself. Every new addition had to be tested and retested because someone would find a way to make it an exploit. Keep in mind, we were breaking some new ground here. It was the most open and dynamic game of it's type. We could have gone the Everquest route and just re-purposed a ten year old MUD with fancy graphics on top, but we didn't.

At the start, nobody could have guessed how bad the behavior was going to be online. Think of UO as a social experiment. The two most common phrases tossed around the office were "a wizard did it", to explain odd game mechanics, and "nazi couches" which we used when talking about how a new feature would be used against other players. If we allowed players to create their own furniture, odds were 100% that somebody would be filling homes with swastika couches...hence "nazi couches".

We made gigantic mistakes along the way. We were too hard on some groups, and too soft on others. We just wanted everyone who played to get a positive experience for their ten bucks. Everyone on the team loved the hell out of UO, and the world of Ultima in general.

So if the bans seemed extreme, they were always done after plenty of debates. They weren't done because the players were insulting to us, or in the case of Rainz, insulting to Richard Garriot. We just wanted keep people from breaking the game for other people.

It was a damn fine game in it's day, though. A damn fine game.

As someone who followed UO2 from the announcement to the cancellation, got any UO2 development stories to share?

Oh god, UO2. Man. I wish people could have seen it. It was glorious fun.

Now, I don't want to say too much since it was almost fifteen years ago and the memory fades. Hell, I have enough problem remembering the names of people I met last month, let alone people I worked with that long ago. I also haven't thought about it it quite some time, so I'm sure I would get many, many details wrong.

We had pretty high spirits back then. Every MMORPG worth it's salt was making money, hand over fist.

UO2 is where Origin first really started feeling the heavy hand of Electronic Arts. They would send down a VP who would have a company meeting, telling us how because he knew hollywood, he knew how to do interactive entertainment. He would then go into closed door meets for the week, and by the end of it people's projects were being shuffled. Just as things calmed down, there would be yet another VP coming in, saying the same things, and repeating the process.

EA didn't like the Ultima franchise. They hated the whole sword and sorcery thing. I remember one high level VP telling me, after the first UO Fan Faire, "we need to stop making games for the kind of person who would wear tights in public". Their money was on the Sims Online, an online car racing game, and a host of other projects that would wind up failing. They were buying developers out left and right, and telling them to make an online game like Origin did...just not with those stupid role playing elements.

Here's the thing. There wasn't an employee there who didn't have some kind of emotional buy in to what we were doing. When I was hired, I went down to Austin for the free trip. I had no intention of going to work for them. Then I pulled up and say the logo "We Create Worlds" and walked into the spacious entry way, seeing all these pieces of my childhood in the cabinets. This was a company I loved, and I didn't want to do anything to tarnish the Ultima name. Pretty much everyone there was like that.

So, UO2 had a number of elements dictated to us from EA's "visionaries". EA wanted more action. More late nineties cool. Demons and sexy babes with machine guns. Robots and explosions. Better graphics. It had to look good. We also needed to make the game easier to play.

It would have been just as bad as it sounds, but everyone there managed to make something great despite the pressures. Yeah, we had rolling cyborg demons with machine guns, but it was still Ultima at heart. There was a reason and a backstory to it. Yeah, we simplified the gameplay, but only in terms of the user interface. Underneath was a game system of complexity and depth, like one would expect for Origin.

I remember the day it was canceled. Started the morning going into my office, only to be pulled into one of the programmers offices. A bunch of people were staring mesmerized at the screen. A big combat hurdle had been beat. Players could now dodge shots. We all kind of cheered as one of the avatars nimbly dodged the fireballs being hurled by someone in a different room. It looked incredible, and felt organic and fun. I was grinning like an idiot as I went back to my office. This game was going to rock. I sat down and opened an e-mail saying there was a company wide meeting scheduled for that afternoon and that attendance was mandatory. The mood became dark as the rumor mill delivered the news.

Everyone spent the rest of that morning gathering up survivors and art work. The back of my car was loaded with swag. (Mostly lost, sadly). That night, word came down that there was going to be a party at Richard Garriot's castle.

Talk about an epic party. Everyone was wearing this t-shirt. We built a giant bonfire, and fed hundreds of thousands of documents and design docs into it. We sat and drank and cried as decades of a once great companies heritage went up in smoke. (Also, drunk and stoned, I backed into someones Jag, damaging the bumper. I don't know whose car it was, and I feel like a jerk for not being brave enough to leave a note.)

Good times.

I am looking to replace the rear pads and rotors on a Pontiac G6. I have replaced the front pads and rotors on a 2001 Jeep Cherokee with little difficulty. However, I noticed that the pins on one side were rusting, but since the Jeep is just a toy at this point and not a daily driver I decided to leave it as is. I am pretty sure they were contributing to uneven brake wear, but i'll worry about it later.

That said, I would have just replaced the rotors and the pads, but now I am wondering if I should be replacing the pins and/or boots too since I'll be under there. Is there anything else for basic maintenance?

Also there isn't a car repair subverses, and this one seemed like the most appropriate subverses.

You want to clean and lubricate the slide pins and replace the boots if needed. If replacing them is easier for you, then do that. Places on the pad that ARE NOT friction material that contacts the caliper or bracket should have a little lube on them as well.
I don't get that last bit. I did it on the Jeep, but what's the point. Are the pads meant to "float" on the caliper? What happens if you don't?

It keeps things moving smoothly with less chance of binding. There's usually a little bit of touching going on as the pad sits in the brackets. Basically, cheap insurance against caliper binding and noise.

When those slider pins seize up the inner pad (the one getting pushed by the piston) is going to do all the stopping, causing reduced brake performance, and causing the inner pad to wear out while the outer does nothing. Hit the pins with brake cleaner, if they are rusty wire wheel them, if they are pitted from rust replace them. Grease the hell out of them with brake grease. Replace the boots if they are fucked up. And yes, the pads are always going to rub slightly when the brake pedal isn't depressed.

So all went well, except for one thing. Clips for the pads are not always included. This meant I had to salvage the old ones. However, I now don't have any rumble (the original issue).

Also, the boots for pins should be in pretty good shape and if you are changing your own brakes you should know if they are going. Mine should be good for a while, so as I change the brakes I'll know when they are wearing out.

Anyway thanks for all advice. I still don't get the lube between the caliper and the pad, but whatever.
